the biochemical and biophysical characterization of the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase enzyme and the development of new antiviral compounds to inhibit this important enzyme.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
NNRTI mutants with reduced RNase H activity are associated with a reduced fitness in cell culture, and that this reduction in fitness is associated with reduced RT content in virions.
reduced fitness of NNRTI mutant virus correlates with low RNase H activity and reduced RT content in virions.
the relative fitness of the mutant viruses correlates with the relative level of RT content and RNase H and RT activities in virions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fitness of NNRTI mutants is determined by a combination of the intrinsic RNase H defect in the mutant protein and the reduction of RT content in virions.
the relative fitness of HIV-1 NNRTI-resistant viruses is determined by the combined effects of RT content and intrinsic RNase H activity of mutant RTs.
the fitness of NNRTI mutant viruses is determined by a complex combination of the intrinsic biochemical activities of mutant RTs and the RT content of virions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relative levels of RT and RNase H in virions are important for viral replication and may be a target for future drug design.
the fitness of HIV-1 variants with NNRTI resistance mutations is determined by the level of virion-associated RT and the RNase H activity of the RT.
NNRTI-resistant RTs with reduced RNase H activity are associated with reduced virus fitness in cell culture.
